conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**Conclusion: The answer is no, not yes.** Current high-quality evidence shows that saw palmetto (Serenoa repens) does **not** improve BPH symptoms beyond placebo in the longer term.

**Key evidence:**

1. **NEJM 2006 (STEP trial):** A year-long randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 225 men with moderate-to-severe BPH symptoms found that saw palmetto was "not superior to placebo for improving urinary symptoms and objective measures" of BPH.
   https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa053085

2. **Cochrane Review (Tacklind et al.):** The authors concluded that Serenoa repens, "at double and triple doses, did not improve urinary flow measures or prostate size in men with lower urinary tract symptoms consistent with BPH."
   https://archive.connect.h1.co/article/717969419/

3. **AAFP 2024 summary of the updated Cochrane review:** States plainly that saw palmetto, alone or combined with other herbal agents, "does not improve urologic symptoms or quality of life in the short term (3 to 6 months) or long term (12 to 17 months)."
   https://www.aafp.org/afp/2024/0500/cochrane-saw-palmetto-benign-prostatic-hyperplasia

4. **CAMUS trial (JAMA 2011):** A large NIH-funded trial escalated saw palmetto doses up to three times the standard amount over 18 months and still found no significant benefit over placebo for BPH symptoms, though it confirmed safety.
   https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3716255/

**Bottom line:** The two largest, most rigorous placebo-controlled trials (STEP and CAMUS) and the Cochrane systematic review all converge on the same conclusion: saw palmetto is well tolerated but provides no clinically meaningful improvement in BPH symptoms compared with placebo, whether in the short or long term.
